lesson.title: From Sample to Population: Reading Polls, Margins of Error, and Valid Inferences
lesson.summary: Learn how to reason from a random sample to a claim about an entire population, including how to apply a stated margin of error, and how to spot survey conclusions that don't hold up.
lesson.body:
Most of the statistics you have studied so far describes data you already have in hand: means, medians, spreads, and probabilities calculated from a complete data set. Inferential statistics asks a different question: given information from only a sample, what can you responsibly say about the entire population that sample was drawn from? This distinction matters because the ACT frequently presents a poll, an experiment, or a survey of a few hundred people and then asks you to reason about a school, a city, or a country of many thousands. The bridge between "what the sample showed" and "what is probably true overall" is built out of two ideas: random selection and margin of error.

A sample is only useful for generalizing to a population if it was chosen randomly, meaning every member of the population had a fair and roughly equal chance of being selected. If a survey about school lunch preferences only questions students in the calculus club, the sample is biased, and no amount of clever math can rescue the conclusion, since the group surveyed is not representative of the whole student body. The ACT often tests this idea directly, asking you to identify why a stated conclusion is flawed; look first at how the sample was gathered before trusting any percentage that came out of it. Once a sample is genuinely random, a second tool, margin of error, tells you how much the sample's result might differ from the true population value just due to the luck of who was chosen. On the ACT, margin of error is almost always given to you as a stated percentage rather than something you calculate from a formula, so your job is to apply it correctly: add and subtract it from the sample statistic to build a plausible range for the population.

Worked example. In a random survey of 200 students at a high school, 120 said they would attend a Friday night trivia event. The survey has a reported margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The high school has 1,500 students total. What range of numbers of students, out of all 1,500, would you expect to say they would attend the event?

Start with the sample proportion: 120 out of 200 said yes, so 120/200 = 0.60, or 60%. Apply the margin of error by subtracting and adding 4 percentage points: 60% - 4% = 56%, and 60% + 4% = 64%. So the true population proportion is plausibly somewhere between 56% and 64%. To convert that into a count of students, multiply each end of the interval by the total population of 1,500: 0.56 x 1,500 = 840, and 0.64 x 1,500 = 960. The survey supports the conclusion that somewhere between 840 and 960 of the 1,500 students would attend the trivia event, not a single exact number.

Two habits will keep you from misreading these problems. First, margin of error attaches to the population estimate, not to the sample count itself, so always convert the sample data to a percentage or proportion before applying the margin of error, and only convert to a count of the full population as the very last step. Second, remember that a wider interval, a bigger margin of error, means less precision, not more information; a poll with a large margin of error can still be honestly reported, it simply supports a weaker, broader conclusion. Watch also for questions that ask you to distinguish correlation from causation: a survey might show that students who eat breakfast tend to have higher test scores, but data gathered by observing rather than controlling who eats breakfast cannot prove that breakfast causes the higher scores. Confirming causation requires a controlled experiment, not just an inferential read of a survey, and the ACT rewards students who catch that distinction.
